phy_edx.5.0.summary: An atom is a tiny, positively charged **nucleus** made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged **electrons**. The nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller in radius than the atom yet holds almost all of its mass, and atoms are about **1 x 10^-10 m** across. Nuclide notation such as 14/6 C shows the **mass (nucleon) number** and the **atomic (proton) number**, and **isotopes** are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Because a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, its overall charge is zero.

core.h: The nuclear model of the atom
core.p: Edexcel wants you to describe an atom as a **positively charged nucleus**, made of **protons and neutrons**, surrounded by **negatively charged electrons**. Two size and mass facts must always be included: the nucleus is tiny compared with the atom, and almost all of the atom's mass is in the nucleus.
bullets: **Nucleus**: at the centre, contains protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge), so the nucleus is positive overall.
**Electrons**: much lighter, negative, found outside the nucleus orbiting it.
The **radius of the nucleus is much smaller than the radius of the atom** (about 1/100 000 of it).
**Almost all of the mass is in the nucleus**, because protons and neutrons are each about 1836 times heavier than an electron.
Most of an atom is therefore **empty space**.
Protons and neutrons together are called **nucleons**.

callouts.p: A positively charged nucleus, consisting of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons, with the radius of the nucleus much smaller than that of the atom and with almost all of the mass in the nucleus.

core.h: Typical sizes: atoms, molecules and nuclei
core.p: Spec point 6.2 asks you to recall the **order of magnitude** of the size of atoms and small molecules. An order of magnitude means the power of ten, so you need the right power of ten, not an exact number.
bullets: Radius of an atom: about **1 x 10^-10 m** (0.1 nm).
Small molecules (for example H2O, CO2): also of order **10^-10 m to 10^-9 m**, a few atoms across.
Radius of a nucleus: about **1 x 10^-15 m**, roughly 10^5 (100 000) times smaller than the atom.
To compare two sizes, divide them: 10^-10 / 10^-15 = 10^5.
Useful link: 1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m, so an atom is about 0.1 nm in radius.

callouts.p: Typical atomic radius = 1 x 10^-10 m. Nuclear radius is about 100 000 times smaller.

core.h: Subatomic particles: relative mass and charge
core.p: Spec point 6.5 asks for the **relative masses** and **relative electric charges** of protons, neutrons, electrons and positrons. Relative means compared with a proton (mass) or with the size of the electron's charge (charge), so there are no units.
bullets: **Proton**: relative mass 1, relative charge +1, found in the nucleus.
**Neutron**: relative mass 1, relative charge 0, found in the nucleus.
**Electron**: relative mass about 1/1836 (often written as 0.0005 or 'negligible'), relative charge -1, found orbiting the nucleus.
**Positron**: the antiparticle of the electron, same relative mass as an electron (1/1836) but relative charge **+1**.
Positrons are not part of ordinary atoms; they are emitted in beta-plus decay (covered later).
Because electrons are so light, the mass of an atom is almost entirely due to its protons and neutrons.

callouts.t: Do not write 0 for the electron's mass
callouts.p: The electron's mass is very small, not zero. Write 1/1836, about 0.0005, or 'very small/negligible'.

core.p: The nucleus contains protons (charge +1 each) and neutrons (charge 0). So the total charge of the nucleus is simply **+1 for every proton**. Neutrons add mass but no charge.
bullets: Charge of nucleus = number of protons x (+1).
A carbon nucleus has 6 protons, so a relative charge of +6.
Each element has its own **characteristic positive nuclear charge**, because each element has its own number of protons.
Neutrons change the mass of a nucleus but never its charge.

callouts.p: The nucleus of each element has a characteristic positive charge, but isotopes of an element differ in mass by having different numbers of neutrons.

core.p: The **atomic number**, also called the **proton number** and given the symbol **Z**, is the number of protons in the nucleus. It is the number that decides which element the atom is.
bullets: Z = number of protons.
Every atom of a given element has the **same Z**: all carbon atoms have Z = 6, all oxygen atoms have Z = 8.
If Z changes, the element changes (this is what happens in some radioactive decays).
In a neutral atom, number of electrons = Z.

callouts.p: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

core.p: The **mass number**, also called the **nucleon number** and given the symbol **A**, is the total number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus. It is called the mass number because protons and neutrons each have relative mass 1, so A is roughly the relative mass of the atom.
bullets: A = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Number of neutrons N = A - Z.
Electrons are **not** counted in A because their mass is negligible.
A is always a whole number and always at least as big as Z.

callouts.p: The total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in the nucleus of an atom.
Neutrons = mass number - atomic number, N = A - Z. This is the most common 1 to 2 mark calculation on this point.

core.p: Edexcel writes nuclei in the format with the **mass number at the top left** and the **atomic number at the bottom left** of the chemical symbol, for example 14/6 C (written as a superscript 14 and subscript 6 before C). In plain text in these notes it is shown as 14/6 C, or carbon-14.
bullets: Top number (larger) = mass (nucleon) number A.
Bottom number (smaller) = atomic (proton) number Z.
Symbol = the element, which is fixed by Z.
Example: 14/6 C has 6 protons, 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons, and 6 electrons when neutral.
Example: 238/92 U has 92 protons and 238 - 92 = 146 neutrons.
Isotopes can also be named by element and mass number: carbon-14, uranium-235.

callouts.p: The bigger number is always on top. If you read 6 as the mass number you will get a negative number of neutrons, which tells you the numbers are the wrong way round.

core.p: **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with **different numbers of neutrons**. So isotopes have the **same atomic number but different mass numbers**. Because they have the same number of protons, they have the same nuclear charge and the same number of electrons, so they behave the same chemically; they differ in mass and often in nuclear stability.
bullets: Same Z, different A, different N.
Carbon-12 (6 p, 6 n), carbon-13 (6 p, 7 n) and carbon-14 (6 p, 8 n) are isotopes of carbon.
Hydrogen-1 (1 p, 0 n), hydrogen-2 deuterium (1 p, 1 n) and hydrogen-3 tritium (1 p, 2 n) are isotopes of hydrogen.
Uranium-235 and uranium-238 are isotopes of uranium (92 protons; 143 and 146 neutrons).
Isotopes have the **same chemical properties** (same electrons) but **different masses**.
Some isotopes are stable; others have unstable nuclei and are radioactive (for example carbon-14). These are called radioisotopes.

callouts.p: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (same atomic number, different mass number).

core.p: In an atom the **number of protons equals the number of electrons**. Each proton has charge +1 and each electron has charge -1, and these charges are equal in size, so they cancel exactly. Neutrons have no charge, so the atom has **no overall charge**: it is **neutral**.
bullets: Total positive charge = number of protons x (+1).
Total negative charge = number of electrons x (-1).
Equal numbers so total charge = 0.
If an atom loses or gains electrons, the numbers are no longer equal and it becomes an **ion** (covered in 6.9).
Neutrons do not affect the overall charge at all.

callouts.p: Say both: the number of protons equals the number of electrons, AND the charge of a proton is equal and opposite to that of an electron, so the charges cancel.

core.h: Where the mass is: putting numbers on it
core.p: Comparing masses shows why almost all the mass is in the nucleus. A carbon-12 atom has 12 nucleons of relative mass 1 (total 12) and 6 electrons of relative mass about 0.0005 each (total about 0.003). So the electrons make up only about 0.03% of the mass.
bullets: Mass of nucleus (C-12): 12 relative units.
Mass of electrons: 6 x 1/1836 = about 0.0033 relative units.
Fraction of mass in nucleus: more than 99.9%.
Yet the nucleus takes up only a tiny fraction of the atom's volume, so the nucleus is extremely **dense**.

core.p: Almost every exam question on this point gives you a nuclide symbol or a table and asks you to fill in protons, neutrons and electrons. Use the same three steps every time.
bullets: Step 1: protons = bottom number Z.
Step 2: neutrons = top number minus bottom number, A - Z.
Step 3: electrons = protons (only if the atom is neutral).
Check: protons + neutrons should equal A.
If you are given an element name but not Z, the element still fixes Z (for example sodium always has 11 protons).

callouts.p: If the question says the particle is an ion, the electron number is NOT equal to the proton number. A positive ion has fewer electrons than protons.

analogy.t: A stadium with a marble on the centre spot
analogy.p: If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be a marble on the centre spot and the electrons would be specks of dust whizzing around the outer stands. Nearly all the mass is in the marble, and the rest is empty space. Isotopes are like marbles made of the same coloured glass (same protons, so same element) but with extra lead balls (neutrons) inside, so they weigh more but look the same from outside. Where it breaks down: electrons are not tiny balls on fixed tracks, the nucleus is not a solid lump, and the real size ratio (about 100 000 to 1) is even more extreme than the stadium suggests.

terms.d: A positively charged nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by negatively charged electrons; overall neutral.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons and almost all its mass.
Subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.
Subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and no charge (relative charge 0).
Subatomic particle orbiting the nucleus with relative mass about 1/1836 and relative charge -1.
The antiparticle of the electron: relative mass about 1/1836 and relative charge +1; emitted in beta-plus decay.
A particle found in the nucleus: a proton or a neutron.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
The number of neutrons in a nucleus, N = A - Z.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Writing a nucleus as its symbol with mass number top left and atomic number bottom left, for example 14/6 C.
Charge compared with the size of the charge on a proton, so proton +1 and electron -1; no units.
Mass compared with the mass of a proton (taken as 1); no units.
The size of a quantity to the nearest power of ten, for example atom radius about 10^-10 m.
Having no overall charge, because the positive and negative charges are equal in size.

mistakes.w: The nucleus contains protons, neutrons and electrons.
mistakes.r: The nucleus contains only protons and neutrons; electrons orbit outside the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Mass number is the number of neutrons.
mistakes.r: Mass (nucleon) number is the number of protons PLUS neutrons; neutrons = A - Z.

mistakes.w: Isotopes have different numbers of protons.
mistakes.r: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

mistakes.w: The electron has no mass / mass 0.
mistakes.r: The electron has a very small relative mass, about 1/1836 (negligible).

mistakes.w: The neutron has a charge of -1.
mistakes.r: The neutron has no charge (relative charge 0).

mistakes.w: The atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and neutrons.
mistakes.r: The atom is neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons, and their charges are equal and opposite.

mistakes.w: Most of the atom's mass is spread through the atom / in the electrons.
mistakes.r: Almost all of the mass is in the nucleus, which is tiny compared with the atom.

mistakes.w: An atom is about 10^-15 m across.
mistakes.r: An atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m; 10^-15 m is the size of a nucleus.

mistakes.w: A positron is a positive proton / has mass 1.
mistakes.r: A positron has the same mass as an electron (1/1836) but a charge of +1.

exam.q: State the relative charge of a neutron.
model: 0 / no charge / neutral
exam.tip: Write 0, not 'none' with a minus sign.

exam.q: Give the typical radius of an atom.
exam.tip: Order of magnitude only; the unit is needed.

exam.q: Complete the table of relative mass and relative charge for the proton, neutron and electron.
model: Proton: mass 1, charge +1
Neutron: mass 1, charge 0
Electron: mass 1/1836 (negligible), charge -1
exam.tip: Usually one mark per correct row.

exam.q: An atom of potassium is written 39/19 K. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
model: Protons = 19
Neutrons = 39 - 19 = 20
Electrons = 19
exam.tip: Electrons equal protons because it is an atom, not an ion.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom.
model: Positively charged nucleus at the centre
Nucleus contains protons and neutrons
Negatively charged electrons orbit / surround the nucleus
Nucleus is very small compared with the atom / almost all the mass is in the nucleus
exam.tip: Include charges, contents, position of electrons and the size/mass point.

exam.q: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
model: Number of protons equals the number of electrons
Charge on proton is equal and opposite to charge on electron, so the charges cancel
exam.tip: Do not mention neutrons balancing anything.

exam.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. Explain what is meant by the term isotopes, using these two atoms as an example.
model: Same number of protons (6)
Different number of neutrons (6 and 8)
So same atomic number but different mass number
exam.tip: Use the numbers given to earn the example mark.

exam.q: Uranium-238 has 92 protons. Write the nuclide symbol for this isotope and state how many neutrons it has.
model: 238/92 U with 238 on top and 92 below
146 neutrons
exam.tip: Mass number top, atomic number bottom.

exam.q: The radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m and the radius of its nucleus is about 1 x 10^-15 m. Calculate how many times larger the atom's radius is than the nucleus's radius.
exam.tip: Divide larger by smaller; no unit for a ratio.

exam.q: Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is in its nucleus even though the nucleus is very small.
model: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus and each has relative mass 1
Electrons have a much smaller (negligible) mass, about 1/1836
exam.tip: Compare the masses of the particles.

exam.q: Two nuclei are 35/17 Cl and 37/17 Cl. Compare the structure of the two nuclei and explain why they are the same element.
model: Both have 17 protons
35/17 Cl has 18 neutrons and 37/17 Cl has 20 neutrons
Different mass numbers so different masses
Same number of protons / same atomic number means same element (same nuclear charge)
exam.tip: Compare means state both similarities and differences with numbers.

exam.q: State how a positron differs from an electron.
model: Positron has a positive charge (+1) whereas the electron has -1 (same mass)
exam.tip: The mass is the same, only the charge sign differs.

worked.q: Complete the particle counts for 27/13 Al (a neutral atom).
steps: Protons = atomic number = 13.
Neutrons = A - Z = 27 - 13 = 14.
Electrons = protons for a neutral atom = 13.
Check: 13 + 14 = 27 = mass number.

worked.q: An atom has 8 protons and 10 neutrons. Write its nuclide notation and name the element, given that oxygen has atomic number 8. Is it an isotope of oxygen-16?
steps: Z = protons = 8, so the element is oxygen.
A = protons + neutrons = 8 + 10 = 18.
Nuclide notation: 18/8 O (18 top left, 8 bottom left).
Oxygen-16 has 8 protons and 8 neutrons; this atom has 8 protons and 10 neutrons.
Same protons, different neutrons, so they are isotopes.
worked.ans: 18/8 O, oxygen-18, which is an isotope of oxygen-16.

worked.q: An atom has a radius of 1.2 x 10^-10 m and its nucleus has a radius of 2.4 x 10^-15 m. How many times bigger is the atom's radius?
steps: Ratio = atomic radius / nuclear radius.
worked.ans: The atom's radius is about 50 000 times bigger than the nucleus's radius.

phy_edx.5.1.summary: In every atom the electrons **orbit the nucleus at different set distances**, and each orbit corresponds to a particular **energy level**. An electron moves to a **higher orbit** (further from the nucleus) when it **absorbs** electromagnetic radiation, and drops back to a **lower orbit** when it **emits** electromagnetic radiation; the energy of the radiation matches the gap between the levels. If an outer electron gains enough energy to leave the atom completely, the atom becomes a **positive ion** because it now has more protons than electrons.

core.p: Spec 6.7: in each atom, the electrons **orbit the nucleus at different set distances** from it. Electrons cannot orbit at just any distance; only certain fixed orbits (also called shells or **energy levels**) are allowed.
bullets: Each allowed orbit is at a **fixed distance** from the nucleus.
The orbits are like rungs on a ladder: an electron can be on one rung or another, but never in between.
Orbits **further from the nucleus** correspond to **higher energy levels**.
The electrons are held in orbit by the **electrostatic attraction** between the negative electrons and the positive nucleus.
Normally electrons fill the lowest available levels (the atom is in its lowest energy state).

callouts.p: Electrons orbit the nucleus at different set distances from the nucleus.

core.p: Each set distance has a definite energy. To move an electron further from the positive nucleus you must do work against the attraction, so an electron in an outer orbit has **more energy** than one in an inner orbit. This is why orbits are called **energy levels**.
bullets: Inner orbit = lower energy level, electron more strongly attracted.
Outer orbit = higher energy level, electron less strongly held.
Moving outwards needs energy to be **supplied** (absorbed).
Moving inwards **releases** energy (emitted).
Because the levels are fixed, the energy changes are fixed amounts too.

core.p: Spec 6.8: electrons change orbit when there is **absorption** or **emission** of electromagnetic radiation. When an electron **absorbs** electromagnetic radiation it gains energy and moves to a **higher orbit, further from the nucleus**. The atom is then said to be **excited**.
bullets: EM radiation carries energy; when absorbed, that energy transfers to the electron.
The electron jumps from a lower energy level to a higher energy level (further out).
Only radiation with the **right amount of energy** (the exact gap between two levels) can be absorbed to make that jump.
Higher frequency EM radiation carries more energy, so larger jumps need higher frequency radiation.
An atom with an electron in a higher-than-normal level is called an **excited atom**.

callouts.p: An electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation and moves to a higher energy level (an orbit further from the nucleus).

fig.cap: Absorption: incoming electromagnetic radiation is absorbed by an electron, which gains energy and moves from a lower orbit to a higher orbit further from the nucleus.

core.p: An excited electron does not stay in the higher level. It falls back to a **lower orbit, closer to the nucleus**, and loses energy by **emitting electromagnetic radiation**. The energy emitted equals the energy difference between the two levels.
bullets: Electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level (closer to the nucleus).
The energy lost is carried away as electromagnetic radiation.
Energy of emitted radiation = energy of higher level - energy of lower level.
Bigger drop = more energy = higher frequency (for example ultraviolet rather than red light).
Electrons may fall back in one big jump or several smaller jumps, each emitting radiation.

callouts.p: An electron falls to a lower energy level (an orbit closer to the nucleus) and emits electromagnetic radiation.

core.p: Absorption and emission are opposite processes. Learn them as a pair so you can write the correct direction and energy change in a 2 or 4 mark explain question.
bullets: Absorption: energy in, electron moves out.
Emission: energy out, electron moves in.
In both, the amount of energy is fixed by the gap between levels.
In both, the radiation involved is **electromagnetic radiation** (for example visible light, ultraviolet).

head: Absorption
Emission
rows: To higher orbit, further from nucleus
To lower orbit, closer to nucleus

callouts.t: Do not say the electron 'emits energy to move up'
callouts.p: Moving up needs energy to be absorbed. Emitting energy always means moving down to a lower level.

core.h: Why only certain frequencies are absorbed or emitted
core.p: Because the orbits are at set distances, the energy gaps between them have fixed values. So an atom can only absorb or emit radiation of particular energies, which means particular **frequencies**. Each element has its own set of energy levels, so it emits its own pattern of frequencies.
bullets: Fixed levels lead to fixed energy gaps.
Fixed energy gaps lead to specific frequencies of EM radiation.
This is why heated elements give out light of particular colours (for example the orange-yellow of sodium street lamps).
Radiation whose energy does not match a gap is not absorbed by that jump.

callouts.p: Explain the chain: set orbits, so set energy levels, so set energy differences, so only specific frequencies are absorbed or emitted.

core.p: Spec 6.9: atoms may form **positive ions** by **losing outer electrons**. If an electron absorbs enough energy, it does not just move to a higher orbit; it escapes from the atom altogether. The atom is left with more protons than electrons, so it has an overall **positive charge**.
bullets: An **ion** is an atom (or molecule) that has lost or gained electrons, so it is charged.
Losing one electron gives a charge of +1; losing two gives +2, and so on.
**Ionisation** is the process of removing electrons from an atom to form an ion.
The number of protons in the nucleus does **not** change; only the number of electrons changes.
So the element stays the same; for example a sodium ion is still sodium.

callouts.p: An atom that has lost one or more (outer) electrons, so it has more protons than electrons and an overall positive charge.

core.h: Why outer electrons are the ones lost
core.p: The outer electrons are furthest from the nucleus, so the electrostatic attraction holding them is weakest, and they are already at a high energy level. They therefore need the **least extra energy** to escape the atom completely.
bullets: Attraction to the nucleus gets weaker with distance.
Outer electrons are also shielded by inner electrons from the full pull of the nucleus.
Less energy is needed to remove an outer electron than an inner one.
So when atoms form positive ions, it is the outer electrons that go.

core.p: Anything that gives an outer electron enough energy can ionise an atom. In this topic the key cause is **ionising radiation**: high-energy electromagnetic radiation or fast-moving particles from radioactive nuclei collide with atoms and knock electrons out.
bullets: Absorbing high-energy EM radiation (for example ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays) can remove an electron.
Collisions with fast particles (for example alpha and beta particles) can knock electrons out.
This is why these radiations are called **ionising radiations** (covered in 6.10 to 6.11).
Lower-energy radiation (for example visible light, radio waves) normally only moves electrons between levels or is not absorbed, rather than removing them.

callouts.p: Excitation: electron moves to a higher orbit but stays in the atom. Ionisation: electron gains enough energy to leave the atom, forming a positive ion.

core.p: To find the charge on an ion, compare protons with electrons. Each proton is +1 and each electron is -1, so charge = protons - electrons.
bullets: Neutral atom: protons = electrons, charge 0.
Positive ion: electrons fewer than protons, charge positive.
Example: an aluminium atom (13 p, 13 e) losing 3 electrons gives Al3+ with 13 p and 10 e, charge +3.
Atoms can also gain electrons to form negative ions, but the Edexcel physics spec focuses on positive ions formed by losing outer electrons.

core.p: Explain questions on this point reward a clear cause and effect chain using the key words **absorb**, **emit**, **higher/lower orbit**, **further from/closer to the nucleus**, **energy level** and **electromagnetic radiation**.
bullets: Always name the radiation as electromagnetic radiation.
Always give the direction: further from or closer to the nucleus.
For ions, say outer electron(s) are lost and the atom now has more protons than electrons.
Say the charge: positive, with the size if you can work it out.
Avoid saying protons are gained to make a positive ion: the nucleus does not change.

callouts.p: absorb / emit, electromagnetic radiation, higher / lower energy level, further from / closer to nucleus, outer electron, positive ion.

analogy.p: Think of electrons as balls that can only rest on the rungs of a ladder (the set orbits). To lift a ball up to a higher rung you must give it exactly the energy to reach that rung (absorption). When the ball drops to a lower rung it gives out that same amount of energy (emission). Throw a ball hard enough and it flies off the top of the ladder completely: that is ionisation, and the ladder is left one ball short, so the atom is positive. Where it breaks down: real electrons are not balls on rungs, the higher rungs of an atom get closer together rather than evenly spaced, and the energy is taken in and given out as electromagnetic radiation, not as a push.

terms.d: A set distance from the nucleus at which an electron can move around the nucleus.
The fixed energy of an electron in a particular orbit; orbits further from the nucleus are higher energy levels.
An electron takes in electromagnetic radiation and moves to a higher orbit, further from the nucleus.
An electron moves to a lower orbit, closer to the nucleus, and gives out electromagnetic radiation.
Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves, such as visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
An atom with an electron in a higher energy level than normal, after absorbing energy.
The lowest energy arrangement of the electrons in an atom.
An atom or molecule that has lost or gained electrons and so is electrically charged.
An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons, so has more protons than electrons.
The process of removing (or adding) electrons to an atom to make an ion.
An electron in the orbit furthest from the nucleus; most easily removed.
The force of attraction between opposite charges, which holds the negative electrons in orbit around the positive nucleus.
The number of waves passing a point per second, in hertz (Hz); higher frequency EM radiation carries more energy.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, forming ions.

mistakes.w: Electrons can orbit at any distance from the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons orbit only at certain set distances (fixed energy levels).

mistakes.w: When an electron absorbs radiation it moves closer to the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Absorbing EM radiation moves the electron to a higher orbit, further from the nucleus.

mistakes.w: When an electron emits radiation it moves to a higher energy level.
mistakes.r: Emitting EM radiation means the electron falls to a lower orbit, closer to the nucleus.

mistakes.w: An atom becomes a positive ion by gaining protons.
mistakes.r: An atom becomes a positive ion by losing (outer) electrons; the number of protons does not change.

mistakes.w: An atom becomes a positive ion by gaining electrons.
mistakes.r: Gaining electrons gives a negative ion; losing electrons gives a positive ion.

mistakes.w: The electron releases energy as sound or heat when it drops.
mistakes.r: The energy is emitted as electromagnetic radiation.

mistakes.w: Any radiation can make an electron jump between levels.
mistakes.r: Only radiation with energy equal to the gap between levels is absorbed for that jump.

mistakes.w: The inner electrons are lost first because they are closer.
mistakes.r: Outer electrons are lost because they are furthest from the nucleus and least strongly attracted.

mistakes.w: An ion is a different element from the atom.
mistakes.r: The proton number is unchanged, so an ion is the same element.

exam.q: State how electrons are arranged in an atom.
model: Electrons orbit the nucleus at (different) set distances / in fixed orbits / energy levels
exam.tip: Use the words set distances or energy levels.

exam.q: Describe what happens to an electron when it absorbs electromagnetic radiation.
model: Electron gains energy
Moves to a higher orbit / energy level further from the nucleus
exam.tip: Give both the energy change and the direction.

exam.q: Describe what happens when an electron moves from an outer orbit to an inner orbit.
model: Electron loses energy
Emits electromagnetic radiation
exam.tip: Name the type of radiation.

exam.q: Explain how an atom can become a positive ion.
model: Atom loses (one or more) outer electron(s)
So it has more protons than electrons / more positive than negative charge
exam.tip: Never say it gains protons.

exam.q: A sodium atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. It loses one electron. State the charge on the ion formed.
exam.tip: Include the plus sign.

exam.q: Explain why atoms only emit electromagnetic radiation of certain frequencies.
model: Electrons are only found at set distances / fixed energy levels
So energy differences between levels are fixed
So only specific energies, and so specific frequencies, of radiation are emitted
exam.tip: Build a chain: levels, gaps, frequencies.

exam.q: Explain why it is the outer electrons that are removed when a positive ion is formed.
model: Outer electrons are furthest from the nucleus
So they are least strongly attracted / need least energy to remove
exam.tip: Link distance to strength of attraction.

exam.q: State what is meant by an ion.
model: An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it is charged
exam.tip: Mention charge.

exam.q: An aluminium atom has 13 protons. It forms an ion with a charge of +3. State the number of electrons in the ion and explain your answer.
model: 10 electrons
13 protons give +13, so 3 electrons lost / 13 - 3 = 10
exam.tip: Charge = protons - electrons.

exam.q: Describe how electrons in an atom can change orbit, and how an atom can become ionised. Use ideas about energy and electromagnetic radiation in your answer.
model: Electrons orbit the nucleus at set distances / energy levels
Orbits further from the nucleus are higher energy levels
Absorbing EM radiation gives an electron energy and it moves to a higher orbit
Electron falls to a lower orbit and emits EM radiation
Energy of radiation equals the difference between the energy levels
If an outer electron absorbs enough energy it leaves the atom
Atom then has more protons than electrons so is a positive ion
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical sequence: orbits, absorption, emission, then ionisation.

worked.q: An electron in an atom moves from energy level 1 to energy level 3, then falls back to level 1 in two steps (3 to 2, then 2 to 1). Describe the energy changes involved.
steps: 1 to 3: the electron moves further from the nucleus, so it must absorb EM radiation with energy equal to the gap between levels 1 and 3.
3 to 2: the electron moves closer to the nucleus and emits EM radiation equal to the gap between levels 3 and 2.
2 to 1: it moves closer again and emits EM radiation equal to the gap between levels 2 and 1.
Total energy emitted in the two steps equals the energy originally absorbed.
worked.ans: One absorption (1 to 3) followed by two emissions (3 to 2 and 2 to 1); each emitted packet has less energy than the absorbed one, but they add up to it.

worked.q: A magnesium atom has 12 protons and 12 electrons. It loses its two outer electrons. State the numbers of protons and electrons in the ion, its charge, and whether it is still magnesium.
steps: Protons are in the nucleus and do not change: 12.
Electrons: 12 - 2 = 10.
Charge = protons - electrons = 12 - 10 = +2.
Element is fixed by the number of protons, which is unchanged.
worked.ans: 12 protons, 10 electrons, charge +2; it is still magnesium (a Mg2+ ion).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain the difference between an excited atom and an ion.
steps: In both cases an electron has absorbed energy.
Excited atom: the electron has moved to a higher energy level (further from the nucleus) but is still in the atom, so the atom is still neutral.
Ion: the electron has gained enough energy to leave the atom completely.
The atom now has more protons than electrons, so it is a positive ion.
worked.ans: An excited atom keeps all its electrons (neutral); an ion has lost an electron and so is charged (positive).

phy_edx.5.2.summary: Unstable nuclei become more stable by emitting **nuclear radiation**: **alpha particles** (helium nuclei), **beta-minus particles** (fast electrons from the nucleus), **beta-plus particles** (positrons), **gamma rays** (high-frequency electromagnetic waves) and **neutrons**. This emission is a **random process**: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next or when, and it is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical changes. Alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma are **ionising radiations**, meaning they can remove electrons from atoms to form ions, which is what makes them both detectable and dangerous.

core.p: Some nuclei are **unstable**: they have the wrong balance of protons and neutrons, or too much energy. An unstable nucleus becomes more stable by **emitting radiation** from the nucleus. This is called **radioactive decay**, and a substance containing unstable nuclei is **radioactive**.
bullets: Spec 6.10: alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus (positron), gamma rays and neutron radiation are **emitted from unstable nuclei** in a **random process**.
The radiation comes from the **nucleus**, not from the electrons around it.
Isotopes with unstable nuclei are called **radioisotopes**.
After decay the nucleus is usually a different, more stable nucleus (except for gamma emission, which only lowers its energy).
Decay is **spontaneous**: it happens without any outside cause.

callouts.p: The random process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation (alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus, gamma or neutrons) to become more stable.

fig.cap: An unstable nucleus can emit five types of nuclear radiation: alpha particles, beta-minus particles (electrons), beta-plus particles (positrons), gamma rays and neutrons. Exactly when a given nucleus decays cannot be predicted.

core.p: Radioactive decay is a **random process**. For any single unstable nucleus it is impossible to predict **when** it will decay, and in a sample it is impossible to predict **which** nucleus will decay next. We can only predict how a large number of nuclei will behave on average.
bullets: Each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in a given time, but the moment of decay is down to chance.
Decay is **not affected** by physical conditions such as temperature or pressure, or by chemical reactions.
Evidence: a Geiger-Muller tube and counter gives **irregular clicks** and the count rate **fluctuates** around an average.
Because it is random, measured counts must be averaged over time or repeated to get reliable values.
With a very large number of nuclei, the overall pattern becomes predictable (this leads to half-life, covered in 6.23 to 6.27).

callouts.p: It cannot be predicted which nucleus will decay next or when a particular nucleus will decay.

core.p: An **alpha particle** is a **helium nucleus**: **2 protons and 2 neutrons** bound together. It has a relative mass of 4 and a relative charge of **+2**. It is emitted by heavy unstable nuclei, for example some isotopes of uranium, radium and americium.
bullets: Symbol: 4/2 He or 4/2 alpha (mass number 4, atomic number 2).
Relative mass 4, relative charge +2.
Contains no electrons, so it is positively charged.
Large, heavy and highly charged, so it interacts strongly with atoms it passes.
Most strongly ionising of the four ionising radiations.
Because it loses energy quickly, it travels only a few centimetres in air and is stopped by a sheet of paper (details in 6.15).

callouts.p: An alpha particle is a helium NUCLEUS (no electrons), not a helium atom.

core.p: A **beta-minus particle** is a **high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus**. It is produced when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton (detail covered in 6.18). Nuclei with too many neutrons tend to be beta-minus emitters, for example carbon-14 and strontium-90.
bullets: Symbol: 0/-1 e or 0/-1 beta.
Relative mass about 1/1836 (negligible), relative charge -1.
It is created in the nucleus at the moment of decay; it is **not** one of the atom's orbiting electrons.
Moderately ionising: less than alpha, more than gamma.
Travels further than alpha, typically stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.

callouts.t: Where does the electron come from?
callouts.p: Write that a beta-minus particle is an electron emitted from the nucleus. Saying it comes from the electron shells loses the mark.

core.p: A **beta-plus particle** is a **positron**: the antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass as an electron but a **positive** charge. It is emitted from the nucleus when a proton changes into a neutron (detail in 6.19). Nuclei with too many protons for stability can be positron emitters, for example fluorine-18 used in PET scans.
bullets: Symbol: 0/+1 e or 0/+1 beta.
Relative mass about 1/1836, relative charge **+1**.
Emitted from the nucleus, like beta-minus.
It is an ionising radiation (spec 6.11).
A positron soon meets an electron and they annihilate (relevant to PET scanning later in the topic).

callouts.p: Same mass (1/1836), opposite charges: beta-minus is an electron (-1), beta-plus is a positron (+1).

core.p: **Gamma rays** are **electromagnetic waves** of very **high frequency** and very short wavelength, emitted from the nucleus. They have **no mass and no charge**. Gamma emission usually happens straight after an alpha or beta decay, when the new nucleus is left with **excess energy**; emitting a gamma ray removes this energy.
bullets: Symbol: 0/0 gamma.
No mass, no charge, travel at the speed of light (3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum).
Part of the electromagnetic spectrum, at the high-frequency end.
Emitting gamma does **not change** the mass number or atomic number of the nucleus.
Weakly ionising, because it is uncharged and interacts with atoms rarely.
Very penetrating: reduced by thick lead or very thick concrete (details in 6.15).

callouts.p: High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from an unstable nucleus, with no mass and no charge.

core.p: Some unstable nuclei, and nuclei that split in nuclear fission, emit **neutrons**. Neutron radiation is a stream of fast **neutrons**: relative mass 1 and **no charge**.
bullets: Symbol: 1/0 n.
Relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
Emitted from unstable nuclei; also released in fission in nuclear reactors (covered in triple 6.38P onwards).
Because it is uncharged it is very penetrating.
Note that the Edexcel spec point 6.11 lists only alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma as ionising radiations; neutrons, being uncharged, do not ionise atoms directly.
Neutrons can be absorbed by other nuclei, which may make those nuclei unstable and so radioactive.

core.p: This table is the single most useful thing to learn for this point. Know what each radiation is, its symbol, relative mass and relative charge.
bullets: Charged particles: alpha (+2), beta-minus (-1), beta-plus (+1).
Uncharged: gamma (a wave) and neutrons (particles).
Massive particles: alpha (4) and neutron (1). Very light: beta-minus and beta-plus.
No mass: gamma.

callouts.p: Top number = mass number, bottom number = charge (or proton number). This is exactly what you need to balance nuclear equations later.

core.p: Spec 6.11: alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma rays are **ionising radiations**. Ionising radiation has enough energy to **remove electrons from atoms** it passes through (or hits), turning neutral atoms into **positive ions**. Each time the radiation ionises an atom it loses some energy, so eventually it is absorbed.
bullets: **Ionisation** = removing an electron from an atom to form a positive ion (links to 6.9).
Charged particles (alpha, beta) ionise by attracting or repelling electrons as they pass close to atoms, and by colliding with them.
Gamma ionises when its energy is absorbed by an electron, which is then knocked out of the atom.
Ionisation is how radiation is **detected** (for example in a Geiger-Muller tube or by darkening photographic film).
Ionisation is also why radiation is **dangerous**: ions formed in living cells can damage DNA and kill or mutate cells (6.29).

callouts.p: Radiation that has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, forming ions.

core.p: How strongly a radiation ionises depends on its **charge** and its **mass/size** (and speed). The more strongly it interacts with atoms, the more ions it makes per centimetre and the faster it loses its energy.
bullets: Alpha: charge +2 and mass 4, so it interacts strongly with nearly every atom near its path: **most ionising**.
Beta-minus and beta-plus: charge of size 1 and tiny mass, so they interact less often: **moderately ionising**.
Gamma: no charge, so it only occasionally interacts: **least ionising** of the four.
Trade-off: **the more ionising a radiation is, the less penetrating it is**, because it uses up its energy over a shorter distance.
The full penetration comparison (paper, aluminium, lead) is covered in 6.15 to 6.16.

callouts.p: Strongly ionising means weakly penetrating, and weakly ionising means strongly penetrating.

core.p: Questions on this point are usually short recall (what is an alpha particle, which radiation has no charge, what does random mean) plus explanations of why radiation is ionising or why decay is random. Use precise words.
bullets: Alpha: say **helium nucleus** or 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
Beta-minus: say **electron emitted from the nucleus** (high-speed).
Beta-plus: say **positron**.
Gamma: say **electromagnetic radiation/wave**, high frequency.
Random: say **cannot predict when** a nucleus will decay or **which** nucleus will decay next.
Ionising: say **removes electrons from atoms** to form ions.

callouts.p: 'Gamma is a particle' or 'alpha is a helium atom' are both marked wrong. Precision is everything on recall questions.

analogy.t: Bowling ball, marbles and a ghost
analogy.p: Imagine rolling things through a crowded room of people holding balloons (the electrons). An alpha particle is a heavy, highly charged bowling ball: it knocks balloons out of almost every hand near its path, so it causes lots of ionisation but stops quickly. Beta particles are small fast marbles: they knock fewer balloons and travel further. Gamma is like a ghost that drifts through and only occasionally grabs a balloon, so it goes a long way. Which person drops a balloon first is random. Where it breaks down: ionisation by charged particles is mostly due to electric forces acting at a distance, not physical bumping, and gamma is a wave rather than an object.

terms.d: A nucleus with an unbalanced number of protons and neutrons or too much energy, which will decay by emitting radiation.
The random process by which an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable.
Impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when a particular nucleus will decay.
A helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, relative mass 4, relative charge +2.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus; relative mass 1/1836, relative charge -1.
A positron emitted from the nucleus; relative mass 1/1836, relative charge +1.
The antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass but a positive charge.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from a nucleus, with no mass and no charge.
Neutrons (relative mass 1, no charge) emitted from unstable nuclei or in fission.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms to form ions.
Removing electrons from an atom, producing a positive ion.
A charged atom formed by losing or gaining electrons.
An isotope with an unstable nucleus, which is radioactive.
How strongly a radiation ionises the atoms it passes; alpha is highest, gamma lowest.
How far radiation can travel through materials before being absorbed; the more ionising, the less penetrating.

mistakes.r: A beta-minus particle is a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus.

mistakes.r: Gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves with no mass and no charge.

mistakes.w: A positron is a positive proton.
mistakes.r: A positron is a positive electron (antiparticle of the electron), mass 1/1836, charge +1.

mistakes.r: Random means you cannot predict which nucleus decays or when; temperature and chemical changes do not affect it.

mistakes.r: Ionising means the radiation removes electrons from atoms, forming ions.

exam.q: State what an alpha particle is made of.
model: 2 protons and 2 neutrons / a helium nucleus
exam.tip: Nucleus, not atom.

exam.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is an electromagnetic wave?
model: Gamma (rays)
exam.tip: The others are particles.

exam.q: Describe the nature of a beta-minus particle and a beta-plus particle.
model: Beta-minus is a (high-speed) electron (emitted from the nucleus)
Beta-plus is a positron (positive electron)
exam.tip: Nature means what it is.

exam.q: State the relative charge of an alpha particle and of a positron.
model: Alpha: +2
Positron: +1
exam.tip: Include signs.

exam.q: Radioactive decay is described as random. State what this means.
model: Cannot predict when a (particular) nucleus will decay / which nucleus will decay next
exam.tip: Avoid 'it happens at random times' without saying unpredictable.

exam.q: Give two pieces of evidence or features that show radioactive decay is random.
model: Count rate from a Geiger-Muller tube fluctuates / clicks are irregular
Rate of decay is not affected by temperature / pressure / chemical change
exam.tip: Fluctuating count rate is the classic answer.

exam.q: Name the four types of nuclear radiation that the specification describes as ionising.
model: Alpha and beta-minus
Beta-plus (positron) and gamma
exam.tip: Neutron radiation is not on this list.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by ionising radiation.
model: Radiation that removes electrons from atoms
Producing (positive) ions
exam.tip: Two ideas: electrons removed, ions formed.

exam.q: Explain why alpha particles are more ionising than gamma rays.
model: Alpha particles have a (large) charge of +2; gamma rays have no charge
Alpha particles have a large mass/size so interact with more atoms
So alpha particles remove electrons from more atoms per cm / lose energy more quickly
exam.tip: Compare both radiations explicitly.

exam.q: Explain why gamma emission does not change the element of the nucleus that emits it.
model: Gamma ray has no mass and no charge
So the number of protons (and neutrons) stays the same / atomic number unchanged
exam.tip: Element is fixed by proton number.

exam.q: Compare alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma radiation in terms of their nature, charge and ionising ability.
model: Alpha is a helium nucleus / 2p + 2n with charge +2
Beta-minus is a fast electron from the nucleus, charge -1
Beta-plus is a positron, charge +1
Gamma is high-frequency EM radiation, no charge or mass
Alpha is most ionising, gamma least ionising, beta in between
Ionising ability linked to charge/mass: greater charge and mass means more ionisation
All four are emitted randomly from unstable nuclei
exam.tip: Organise by radiation, then make a clear comparison sentence about ionisation.

worked.q: A student says: 'If I cool a radioactive sample in a freezer I can slow down its decay, and I can tell which atom will decay next.' Write a model correction.
steps: Radioactive decay is a random process happening in the nucleus.
It is not affected by physical conditions such as temperature, so freezing has no effect on the rate.
Random means it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when.
We can only predict the average behaviour of a large number of nuclei.
worked.ans: Both claims are wrong: decay rate is unaffected by temperature, and which nucleus decays next cannot be predicted.

worked.q: Identify each radiation from its description: (a) relative mass 4, charge +2; (b) no mass, no charge; (c) relative mass 1/1836, charge +1; (d) relative mass 1, charge 0; (e) relative mass 1/1836, charge -1.
steps: (a) Mass 4 and charge +2: 2 protons + 2 neutrons, so an alpha particle.
(b) No mass, no charge: an electromagnetic wave, so gamma.
(c) Tiny mass, positive: a positron, so beta-plus.
(d) Mass 1, uncharged: neutron radiation.
(e) Tiny mass, negative: an electron, so beta-minus.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain how a beta-minus particle passing through air can be detected using the idea of ionisation.
steps: The beta-minus particle is charged (-1) and moving fast.
As it passes air molecules it repels and knocks out electrons, so it is ionising.
This creates positive ions and free electrons along its path.
A detector such as a Geiger-Muller tube responds to these ions (each ionisation event gives a pulse, heard as a click).
worked.ans: Beta-minus ionises gas atoms by removing electrons; the ions produced are what the detector registers.

phy_edx.5.3.summary: **Background radiation** is the low-level ionising radiation that is around us all the time, from natural sources on Earth and in space plus a small man-made contribution. The biggest UK source is **radon gas** seeping out of rocks such as granite; others are rocks and building materials, food and drink, **cosmic rays** from space and medical X-rays. Radioactivity is detected with **photographic film** (which darkens when exposed) or a **Geiger-Muller tube** connected to a counter, and every count must be **corrected by subtracting the background count rate**.

core.p: Wherever you are, a radiation detector clicks even with no radioactive source nearby. That ever-present radiation is **background radiation**. It is ionising radiation (alpha, beta and gamma, plus cosmic ray particles) from sources that are always there, so it can never be switched off or completely removed.
bullets: It is **always present** and comes from **natural** and **man-made** sources
Most of it (well over 80% in the UK) is **natural**
It is **low level** - normally too small to cause noticeable harm, but it still carries a small risk
Because radioactive decay is **random**, the background count rate fluctuates from second to second
Its size **varies with location** (rocks underground, altitude) and with **lifestyle** (flying, medical scans)

callouts.p: Ionising radiation that is present around us all the time, from natural sources (such as rocks, radon gas and cosmic rays) and man-made sources (such as medical X-rays and nuclear fallout).

core.h: Origins from the Earth: radon gas
core.p: Rocks such as **granite** contain small amounts of uranium. As uranium decays, one of the products is **radon**, a radioactive gas. Because it is a gas it seeps out of the ground and can collect in houses, especially in cellars and poorly ventilated rooms.
bullets: **Radon gas** is the **largest single source** of background radiation in the UK (about half)
Radon is an **alpha emitter**; breathing it in exposes the **lungs** to alpha particles from inside the body
Levels are highest in granite areas such as **Cornwall** and Devon, and parts of Scotland
Homes can be protected by **ventilation** and by sealing floors or fitting under-floor fans
It is natural, so it comes under sources from Earth

callouts.p: In the UK, radon gas from rocks is the biggest contributor to background radiation.

core.h: Origins from the Earth: rocks, soil and buildings
core.p: The ground under our feet and the materials buildings are made from contain naturally radioactive isotopes (of uranium, thorium and potassium). These give out gamma rays all the time.
bullets: **Rocks and soil** contain radioactive isotopes left over from when the Earth formed
**Building materials** made from rock (stone, brick, concrete) emit radiation indoors
Granite buildings give a higher dose than wooden ones
These are all **natural** sources from the Earth

core.h: Origins from the Earth: food, drink and our bodies
core.p: Living things take in radioactive isotopes along with ordinary ones, because isotopes of an element behave the same way chemically. So our food, drink and even our own bodies are slightly radioactive.
bullets: **Potassium-40** is found in foods such as bananas, nuts and potatoes
**Carbon-14** is present in all living things
Some isotopes get into water and plants from the soil
The human body itself contains small amounts of radioactive isotopes

callouts.p: If asked why food is radioactive: plants absorb radioactive isotopes from the soil, air and water, and these pass along food chains.

core.p: **Cosmic rays** are high-energy particles (mostly protons) and radiation that come from the **Sun** and from **outer space** (exploding stars and other galaxies). The Earth's **atmosphere** absorbs much of them, so the dose at ground level is fairly small.
bullets: Cosmic rays come **from the Sun and stars**, not from the Earth
The atmosphere acts as a **shield**: less air above you means more cosmic radiation
So the dose is **higher at high altitude** - on mountains and in aircraft
**Pilots and aircrew** receive a larger yearly dose than people on the ground
The Earth's magnetic field also deflects many charged cosmic ray particles

callouts.p: Cosmic rays are from space. Ultraviolet from the Sun is not counted as background ionising radiation in these questions.

core.p: A small part of background radiation comes from human activity. Medical uses are by far the largest of these.
bullets: **Medical**: X-rays, CT scans and radioactive tracers (about 15% of the UK average)
**Nuclear power** and the nuclear industry: small leaks and waste (well under 1%)
**Fallout** from past nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere
**Nuclear accidents** such as Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011)
Some industrial and research sources

callouts.p: Nuclear power stations contribute only a tiny fraction of the average background dose.

core.p: Exam questions often give a pie chart and ask which sources are natural, which are man-made, and which is the biggest. Learn the split.
bullets: Natural: radon, rocks and buildings, food and drink, cosmic rays
Man-made: medical, nuclear industry, weapons fallout, accidents
Natural sources make up roughly 85% of the total in the UK

core.p: The background dose a person gets depends on where they live and what they do. Each difference links back to a source.
bullets: **Underlying rock**: granite areas release more radon and gamma, so a higher count
**Altitude**: less atmosphere to absorb cosmic rays, so a higher count up mountains or in planes
**Home**: poor ventilation lets radon build up; stone houses emit more than wooden ones
**Job**: aircrew, radiographers and nuclear workers may receive more
**Medical treatment**: a CT scan can give more than a year of natural background in one go

callouts.p: Always link the reason to the source: 'higher because granite contains uranium which decays to radon gas'.

core.p: A detector always picks up background radiation as well as the source you are studying. To find the count rate due to the source alone you must measure the background first and subtract it.
bullets: Measure the background count with the **source removed** (and stored away)
Measure for a **long time** (e.g. several minutes) and find the mean, because decay is random
Then measure with the source in place
**Corrected count rate = measured count rate - background count rate**
Use the same units for both (counts per second or counts per minute)
Forgetting to subtract background gives answers that are too high, especially when the source is weak

callouts.p: corrected count rate = measured count rate - background count rate
Convert counts in a time into a count rate first: 900 counts in 10 minutes is 90 counts per minute, or 1.5 counts per second.

core.p: Radiation affects photographic film in the same way that light does: it **darkens (exposes) the film**. The more radiation absorbed, the darker the film when it is developed. This was how radioactivity was first discovered (Becquerel, 1896).
bullets: Used in **film badges** worn by people who work with radiation (radiographers, nuclear workers)
The badge is kept in a light-proof case so only ionising radiation affects the film
Different **windows/filters** (open, plastic, aluminium, lead) let you work out which type of radiation and how much
The film is developed regularly; **darker film = bigger dose**
Disadvantage: it does **not give an instant reading** - it shows the dose only after it has been received
Advantage: cheap, light, and gives a permanent record of the total dose

callouts.p: Ionising radiation causes photographic film to darken; the amount of darkening shows how much radiation has been received.

core.p: A **Geiger-Muller (GM) tube** connected to a **counter** (or ratemeter) gives an instant measurement. Each time radiation enters the tube and ionises the gas inside, a pulse of current is produced, which the counter records as one **count** (and a speaker may click).
bullets: Radiation enters through a **thin window** at the end of the tube
It **ionises** the low-pressure gas (such as argon) inside
A high voltage between the central wire and the tube wall makes the ions and electrons move, producing a **pulse of current**
The counter adds up the pulses: the **count**; counts per second or per minute is the **count rate**
Higher count rate = more radiation reaching the tube (more intense source, or detector closer)
It gives a **reading straight away**, unlike film
It does not by itself say which type of radiation it is - you need absorbers to find out

callouts.p: The number of counts (radiation detections) recorded per second or per minute.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to choose a detector for a job and justify it.
bullets: Need an instant reading or to find a source or leak: **GM tube**
Need a record of a worker's total dose over a month: **film badge**

core.p: Radioactive decay is **random**, so a count over a short time can be unusually high or low. Repeated or long measurements give a more **reliable** mean value.
bullets: Take counts over a **longer time** to reduce the effect of random fluctuations
**Repeat** readings and calculate a **mean**
Keep the distance between source and detector the same
Background varies slightly too, so measure it on the same day in the same place

callouts.p: In practical questions, 'measure background first, then subtract it' and 'repeat and take a mean' are almost always credited.

analogy.p: Background radiation is like the constant murmur of a classroom: chairs scraping, a humming projector, traffic outside. If you want to measure how loud one student is, you first measure the noise with that student silent, then subtract it. Radon is the noisy radiator in the corner, cosmic rays are the traffic outside. The analogy breaks down because sound is not ionising and cannot harm cells, and background radiation is random in a way that classroom noise is not: you cannot predict which atom will decay next.

terms.d: Ionising radiation that is around us all the time from natural and man-made sources.
A radioactive gas, an alpha emitter, produced by the decay of uranium in rocks such as granite; the largest UK background source.
A rock containing uranium, so areas built on it have higher background radiation.
High-energy particles and radiation from the Sun and outer space, partly absorbed by the atmosphere.
A source of radiation not caused by humans, e.g. rocks, radon, food, cosmic rays.
A source caused by human activity, e.g. medical X-rays, nuclear power, weapons fallout.
Radioactive material spread into the environment by nuclear weapons tests or accidents.
Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, forming ions.
Film that darkens when exposed to ionising radiation; the darkness shows the dose received.
A badge containing photographic film behind different filters, worn to record a worker's radiation dose.
A gas-filled tube in which ionising radiation causes pulses of current that a counter records.
One detection of radiation recorded by a GM tube and counter.
Number of counts per second or per minute.
Measured count rate minus background count rate; the count rate due to the source alone.
Cannot be predicted for an individual nucleus; causes fluctuations in counts.
Height above sea level; greater altitude means less atmosphere shielding from cosmic rays.

mistakes.w: Background radiation mainly comes from nuclear power stations.
mistakes.r: Nuclear power contributes well under 1%; most comes from natural sources, with radon gas the largest.

mistakes.w: Background radiation can be removed by switching off sources.
mistakes.r: It is always present because most of it is natural; it can only be measured and subtracted.

mistakes.w: Cosmic rays come from the Earth's core.
mistakes.r: Cosmic rays come from space (the Sun and stars).

mistakes.w: You add background to the reading.
mistakes.r: Corrected count rate = measured count rate minus background count rate.

mistakes.w: A Geiger counter measures the type of radiation.
mistakes.r: A GM tube counts ionising events; absorbers are needed to identify the type.

mistakes.w: Film badges show the dose straight away.
mistakes.r: Film must be developed, so it only shows the dose received afterwards.

mistakes.w: People on planes get more radiation because they are closer to the Sun.
mistakes.r: They are above much of the atmosphere, which normally absorbs cosmic rays.

mistakes.w: Radon is a gamma emitter that comes from the air.
mistakes.r: Radon is a radioactive gas (alpha emitter) released from rocks such as granite.

mistakes.w: Measuring background for 10 seconds is enough.
mistakes.r: Decay is random, so measure for a long time or repeat and find a mean.

exam.q: What is meant by background radiation?
model: Ionising radiation that is present all the time / everywhere
From natural and man-made sources (named example)
exam.tip: Two ideas: always present, and where it comes from.

exam.q: Name the source that contributes most to background radiation in the UK.
model: Radon gas
exam.tip: Just 'rocks' is not enough if the pie chart lists radon separately.

exam.q: Give one source of background radiation from space and one from the Earth.
model: Space: cosmic rays (from the Sun/stars)
Earth: radon gas / rocks such as granite / soil / building materials / food
exam.tip: The spec asks for origins from Earth and space, so expect this split.

exam.q: Explain why airline pilots receive a higher dose of background radiation than people working at ground level.
model: They spend time at high altitude
Less atmosphere above to absorb cosmic rays, so more cosmic radiation reaches them
exam.tip: Name cosmic rays and the shielding by the atmosphere.

exam.q: A GM tube measures 1200 counts in 5 minutes near a source. The background count rate is 30 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate.
model: Measured count rate = 1200 / 5 = 240 counts per minute
Corrected = 240 - 30
= 210 counts per minute
exam.tip: Turn the count into a rate before subtracting.

exam.q: Describe how a Geiger-Muller tube and counter detect radiation.
model: Radiation enters the tube (through the thin window)
It ionises the gas inside the tube
This produces a pulse of current which is recorded as a count by the counter
exam.tip: Ionisation of the gas is the key word.

exam.q: Explain how photographic film is used to monitor the radiation received by hospital workers.
model: Workers wear a badge containing photographic film
Ionising radiation darkens the film
The film is developed regularly; the darker the film the greater the dose received
exam.tip: Add that filters show the type of radiation for a fourth idea.

exam.q: Give one advantage of a GM tube compared with photographic film.
model: Gives an instant/immediate reading (count rate)
exam.tip: Contrast instant reading with having to develop film.

exam.q: Suggest why background radiation is higher in Cornwall than in London.
model: Cornwall has a lot of granite rock (which contains uranium)
Which releases (more) radon gas / emits more radiation
exam.tip: Link the location to granite and radon.

exam.q: A student wants to measure the count rate from a weak radioactive source. Describe how she should take account of background radiation and make her result reliable.
model: Remove the source and measure the background count with the GM tube
Over a long time / repeat and find the mean (because decay is random)
Measure the count rate with the source in place
Subtract the background count rate from the measured count rate
exam.tip: Sequence: background first, source second, subtract.

exam.q: Discuss the sources of background radiation, explaining why the dose a person receives can vary. (6 marks)
model: Background radiation is ionising radiation present all the time
Natural sources from the Earth: radon gas from rocks such as granite, rocks/soil/building materials, food and drink
Natural source from space: cosmic rays from the Sun and stars
Man-made sources: medical X-rays/scans, nuclear industry, weapons fallout, accidents
Dose varies with location: granite areas have more radon; higher altitude gives more cosmic rays
Dose varies with lifestyle: flying, medical treatment, job, ventilation of home
exam.tip: Structure: definition, natural Earth, space, man-made, then reasons for variation.

worked.q: A source gives 3600 counts in 2 minutes. With the source removed, the detector records 600 counts in 20 minutes. Calculate the corrected count rate in counts per second.
steps: Measured rate = 3600 / 120 s = 30 counts per second
Background rate = 600 / 1200 s = 0.5 counts per second
Corrected rate = 30 - 0.5

worked.q: A worker's film badge has an open window, an aluminium window and a lead window. After developing, the film is dark under the open window and the aluminium window, and slightly grey under the lead. What radiation was the worker exposed to?
steps: Radiation reached the film behind aluminium, so it was not only beta (beta is stopped by a few mm of aluminium)
Some radiation got through lead, which only gamma can do
The open and aluminium windows are similarly dark, so there was little beta

worked.q: Explain why a family living in a granite house in Cornwall with a sealed, unventilated cellar receives a larger background dose than average.
steps: Granite contains uranium, which decays to radon gas
Radon seeps out of the ground and building stone and builds up in the unventilated cellar
Breathing radon exposes the lungs to alpha radiation; the granite walls also emit gamma
worked.ans: More radon and more radiation from the rock and building material, so a bigger dose; ventilation would reduce it.
