phy_edx.5.4.summary: Unstable nuclei emit three main kinds of nuclear radiation: an **alpha particle** (equivalent to a **helium nucleus**, 2 protons and 2 neutrons), a **beta particle** (an **electron emitted from the nucleus**; the beta-plus version is a positron) and a **gamma ray** (**electromagnetic radiation**). They differ in charge and mass, which explains how strongly they **ionise** and how far they **penetrate**. Alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating (stopped by paper), beta is in between (stopped by a few mm of aluminium) and gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating (only reduced by several cm of lead).

core.h: Three kinds of radiation from the nucleus
core.p: All three types are given out by **unstable nuclei** as they decay. They are all **ionising radiations**, but they are very different things: two are particles with mass and charge, one is a wave.
bullets: **Alpha (α)**: a particle equivalent to a **helium nucleus**
**Beta (β- )**: a fast **electron emitted from the nucleus**
**Positron (β+)**: the positive version of beta, a positron emitted from the nucleus
**Gamma (γ)**: a high-frequency **electromagnetic wave**
Their **charge**, **mass** and **energy** decide how they behave in matter

callouts.p: An alpha particle is equivalent to a helium nucleus; a beta particle is an electron emitted from the nucleus; a gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation.

core.p: An alpha particle is made of **2 protons and 2 neutrons** bound together, exactly the same as the nucleus of a helium atom. It has no electrons, so it carries a **charge of +2**.
bullets: Relative mass **4**, relative charge **+2**
Symbol: 4 over 2 He (or 4 over 2 α)
The **heaviest** and **most highly charged** radiation
Moves relatively slowly compared with beta and gamma
**Strongly ionising**; **weakly penetrating**
Range of only a **few cm in air**; stopped by a **sheet of paper** or the outer layer of dead skin

callouts.p: Do not write 'a helium atom'. It is a helium nucleus: it has no electrons.

core.p: A beta-minus particle is a **high-speed electron that comes from the nucleus**, not from the electron shells. It is created when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton. A beta-plus particle is a **positron**: the same mass as an electron but a positive charge.
bullets: Beta-minus: relative charge **-1**, relative mass about **1/1840** (almost zero)
Positron (beta-plus): relative charge **+1**, same tiny mass
Symbol for beta-minus: 0 over -1 e; for a positron: 0 over +1 e
**Moderately ionising** and **moderately penetrating**
Range up to about **a metre in air**; passes through paper; stopped by **a few mm of aluminium**

callouts.p: The beta electron is made in and emitted from the nucleus. The atom's orbiting electrons are not involved.

core.p: Gamma rays are **electromagnetic radiation** of very high frequency and very short wavelength, at the top end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They are emitted when a nucleus gets rid of extra energy, often just after an alpha or beta decay.
bullets: **No mass** and **no charge**
Travel at the **speed of light** (3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum)
Emitting gamma does **not change** the mass number or atomic number
**Weakly ionising**; **highly penetrating**
Passes through paper and aluminium; intensity only **reduced** by **several cm of lead** or **thick concrete**
Travels a very long way in air

core.p: This is the table to learn by heart. Exam questions often give part of it with gaps.
bullets: Pattern: as you go alpha to beta to gamma, **ionising power falls** and **penetrating power rises**

core.p: Radiation **ionises** an atom when it knocks one or more **electrons** out of it, leaving a **positive ion**. Every ionisation uses up some of the radiation's energy. So ionising and penetrating are connected: the more ionisations per centimetre, the faster the energy is used up and the shorter the distance travelled.
bullets: Ionisation = removing electrons from atoms to form ions
Each collision transfers energy from the radiation to the material
When all its energy is used, the radiation is **absorbed** (stopped)
Ionisation in living cells can damage DNA, which is why radiation is dangerous

callouts.p: How readily the radiation knocks electrons out of atoms it passes, forming ions.
How far the radiation can travel through a material before it is absorbed.

core.h: Why alpha is so strongly ionising
core.p: Alpha particles are **large**, **slow** and carry a **+2 charge**. The strong charge pulls hard on electrons in nearby atoms, and because the particle moves slowly it spends longer near each atom. It therefore produces a huge number of ions in a short distance.
bullets: Large charge (+2): strong electrostatic pull on electrons
Large mass and relatively slow: more time near each atom
Many ionisations per mm, so it **loses its energy very quickly**
Result: **short range** - stopped by paper or a few cm of air

callouts.p: Say: 'alpha is the most ionising, so it transfers its energy quickly and is stopped in a short distance - that is why it is the least penetrating'.

core.p: Gamma rays have **no charge** and **no mass**, so they rarely interact with the atoms they pass. They produce very few ions per cm, lose energy slowly and can travel through a lot of material.
bullets: No charge: no electrostatic pull on electrons
Few interactions, so **weakly ionising**
Energy lost slowly, so **highly penetrating**
Lead is a good absorber because it is very **dense** with lots of electrons to interact with
Gamma is never completely 'stopped' - the intensity is reduced

core.p: Beta particles have a **smaller charge (-1)** than alpha and a **tiny mass**, and they travel very fast. They ionise less often than alpha, so they travel further, but they are charged so they still ionise more than gamma.
bullets: Charge -1, so weaker interaction than alpha
Very fast and very light: less time near each atom
Moderately ionising, so moderately penetrating
Stopped by a few mm of aluminium

callouts.p: The more strongly a radiation ionises, the less penetrating it is.

core.p: You can work out which radiation a source emits by placing different absorbers between the source and a **GM tube** and seeing what makes the count rate fall.
bullets: Measure the **background count rate** first and subtract it from every reading
Keep the **distance** between source and detector fixed (alpha only travels a few cm, so keep it close)
Record the count rate with **no absorber**, then **paper**, **aluminium (few mm)**, **lead (few cm)**
Big drop with paper: **alpha** present
Further drop with aluminium: **beta** present
Count that remains through aluminium and is reduced by lead: **gamma** present
Use tongs, keep the source away from the body, return it to its lead box quickly

head: Count rate falls when you add...
Radiation present
rows: Still a count after aluminium, reduced by lead

callouts.p: If the count rate after lead equals the background, there is no gamma - not 'lead stopped everything'.

core.h: Charge shown by deflection in fields
core.p: Because alpha and beta are charged, they are **deflected** by electric and magnetic fields; gamma is not. This is evidence for their charges.
bullets: Alpha (+) bends **towards the negative plate**
Beta-minus (-) bends **towards the positive plate**, in the opposite direction to alpha
Beta is deflected **much more** than alpha because its mass is so much smaller
Gamma is **not deflected** because it has no charge

core.h: Using the properties to explain hazards and uses
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to apply ionising and penetrating power to a situation.
bullets: **Outside the body**: alpha is stopped by skin, so least harmful; beta and gamma can reach organs
**Inside the body** (swallowed or breathed in): alpha is most harmful because it is the most ionising and all its energy is deposited in a small region of cells
Smoke detectors use alpha because it ionises air strongly but cannot escape the casing
Paper thickness gauges use beta because it partly passes through paper
Medical tracers and sterilising use gamma because it can pass out of the body or through packaging

callouts.p: Pick the radiation whose penetration matches the job, then justify with ionising/penetrating power.

analogy.t: Bowling ball, tennis ball and ghost
analogy.p: Imagine running through a crowded room. Alpha is a huge, slow bowling ball with a strong pull: it crashes into everyone near it (lots of ionising) but stops after a few steps (low penetration). Beta is a fast tennis ball: it hits fewer people and gets further. Gamma is almost a ghost: it rarely touches anyone, so it gets right across the room. The analogy breaks down because gamma is a wave, not a ball, and radiation does not bounce off people - it removes electrons from atoms and transfers energy each time.

terms.d: Two protons and two neutrons; equivalent to a helium nucleus; charge +2, mass 4.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus; charge -1, very small mass.
A particle with the mass of an electron and charge +1, emitted from the nucleus.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from a nucleus; no mass, no charge.
A nucleus that may decay by emitting radiation to become more stable.
Removing electrons from atoms (or molecules) so that they become ions.
An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it is charged.
How strongly radiation ionises atoms it passes; alpha strongest, gamma weakest.
How far radiation travels through a material before being absorbed; gamma most, alpha least.
Material placed in the path of radiation to absorb it, e.g. paper, aluminium, lead.
The distance radiation travels in a material before being absorbed.
Transverse waves of electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light.
Charge compared with a proton: alpha +2, beta -1, positron +1, gamma 0.
Number of counts per second or per minute recorded by a detector.

mistakes.w: An alpha particle is a helium atom.
mistakes.r: It is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons, no electrons).

mistakes.w: A beta particle is an electron from the outer shell of the atom.
mistakes.r: A beta particle is an electron emitted from the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Gamma is a particle with no mass.
mistakes.r: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation (a wave).

mistakes.w: Gamma is the most ionising because it is the most dangerous.
mistakes.r: Gamma is the least ionising; alpha is the most ionising.

mistakes.w: Lead stops gamma completely.
mistakes.r: Several cm of lead greatly reduces (absorbs most of) gamma.

mistakes.w: Beta is stopped by paper.
mistakes.r: Beta passes through paper; it is stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

mistakes.w: Alpha is the most penetrating because it is the biggest.
mistakes.r: Alpha is the least penetrating because it ionises strongly and loses its energy quickly.

mistakes.w: Alpha is harmless.
mistakes.r: Alpha is harmless only outside the body; inside the body it is the most dangerous.

mistakes.w: Forgetting background in absorber experiments.
mistakes.r: Subtract the background count rate from each reading.

exam.q: State what an alpha particle is.
model: A helium nucleus / 2 protons and 2 neutrons
exam.tip: 'Helium atom' gets zero.

exam.q: State what a beta-minus particle is.
model: An electron emitted from the nucleus (fast-moving)
exam.tip: Include 'from the nucleus'.

exam.q: Which type of radiation is part of the electromagnetic spectrum?
model: Gamma
exam.tip: Alpha and beta are particles.

exam.q: Which radiation is the most ionising? Give a reason.
model: Alpha
It has the largest charge (+2) / largest mass so interacts strongly with atoms
exam.tip: Reason must refer to charge or mass.

exam.q: State what is needed to absorb (a) alpha (b) beta (c) gamma radiation.
model: (a) paper / a few cm of air / skin
(b) a few mm of aluminium
(c) several cm of lead / thick concrete (reduces it)
exam.tip: Give a material and a thickness.

exam.q: Explain why alpha radiation has a much shorter range in air than gamma radiation.
model: Alpha is strongly ionising (gamma weakly ionising)
Each ionisation transfers energy, so alpha loses its energy quickly
So alpha is stopped after a short distance; gamma loses energy slowly and travels much further
exam.tip: The chain: ionise, lose energy, stop.

exam.q: A source is placed 3 cm from a GM tube. Corrected count rates: no absorber 400 counts/s, paper 400 counts/s, 3 mm aluminium 120 counts/s, 2 cm lead 30 counts/s. Which radiations does the source emit? Explain.
model: No alpha: paper causes no drop
Beta present: aluminium reduces count rate a lot
Gamma present: count rate still present after aluminium
Lead reduces the gamma (but does not stop it)
exam.tip: Work through each absorber in turn.

exam.q: Compare the ionising and penetrating abilities of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
model: Alpha most ionising, gamma least ionising, beta in between
Alpha least penetrating (stopped by paper)
Beta moderately penetrating (stopped by a few mm aluminium)
Gamma most penetrating (reduced by thick lead); the more ionising the less penetrating
exam.tip: 'Compare' needs comparative words for both properties.

exam.q: Explain why a beam of radiation from a source splits into three when it passes between charged plates.
model: Alpha is positive so is deflected towards the negative plate
Beta is negative so is deflected towards the positive plate, more than alpha (smaller mass)
Gamma has no charge so is not deflected
exam.tip: Link each deflection to charge.

exam.q: Explain why alpha sources are dangerous inside the body but much less dangerous outside it.
model: Outside, alpha is absorbed by the dead outer layer of skin/clothes so cannot reach living cells
Inside, alpha is highly ionising so it damages the nearby cells strongly
exam.tip: Use ionising and penetrating in the same answer.

exam.q: Describe how you would use a GM tube and absorbers to find out which type(s) of radiation a sealed source emits. Include how you would make the results valid and how you would work safely. (6 marks)
model: Measure background count rate with source absent
Place source a short fixed distance (a few cm) from GM tube; measure count rate with no absorber
Repeat with paper, then a few mm of aluminium, then several cm of lead
Subtract background from each reading; repeat and average (decay is random)
Drop with paper means alpha; drop with aluminium means beta; count remaining through aluminium, reduced by lead, means gamma
Safety: handle with tongs, keep at arm's length, minimise exposure time, store in lead box
exam.tip: Cover method, analysis and safety for full marks.

worked.q: A source gives these readings (counts per minute): background 20; no absorber 520; paper 515; 5 mm aluminium 22; 5 cm lead 21. Identify the radiation.
steps: Correct each reading: no absorber 500, paper 495, aluminium 2, lead 1
Paper hardly changes the count (495 vs 500, within random variation): no alpha
Aluminium reduces the count almost to zero: beta present
After aluminium the corrected count is about zero: no gamma
worked.ans: The source emits beta radiation only.

worked.q: Explain, using ionising and penetrating power, why gamma is used to sterilise sealed packs of surgical instruments rather than alpha.
steps: The radiation must pass through the packaging to reach microorganisms on the instruments
Alpha is weakly penetrating and would be absorbed by the packaging
Gamma is highly penetrating so it passes through the packaging and kills the microorganisms
worked.ans: Gamma, because only it penetrates the sealed packaging; the pack can stay sealed so the instruments stay sterile.

worked.q: Compare the relative charge and mass of an alpha and a beta-minus particle, and use this to explain which is deflected more in an electric field.
steps: Alpha: charge +2, mass 4; beta: charge -1, mass about 1/1840
Alpha has twice the charge but about 7000 times the mass
Force depends on charge; a large mass makes a particle much harder to deflect
worked.ans: Beta is deflected much more (in the opposite direction to alpha) because its mass is so small.

phy_edx.5.5.summary: The model of the atom has changed as **new experimental evidence** appeared. Dalton's solid sphere was replaced by Thomson's **plum pudding model** (a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it) after the electron was discovered. Rutherford's **alpha particle scattering experiment** showed that most of the atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positive **nucleus**, giving the nuclear model, and **Bohr** then improved it by placing electrons in **fixed orbits (energy levels)** at set distances from the nucleus.

core.p: A scientific model is a simplified picture used to explain observations and make predictions. When an experiment produces results that a model **cannot explain**, scientists change or replace the model. The atom is the classic example: each new model was accepted because it explained more of the evidence.
bullets: A model must explain **all** the available evidence
New technology allows new experiments, giving **new evidence**
If results do not match a model's **predictions**, the model is changed
New ideas are checked by other scientists (**peer review**) and by repeating experiments
Old models are not 'wrong and useless' - they were the best explanation for the evidence at the time

callouts.p: Describe how and why the atomic model has changed, including the plum pudding model and Rutherford alpha particle scattering leading to the Bohr model.

core.p: In the early 1800s John Dalton described atoms as **tiny solid spheres** that could not be divided, with each element having its own kind of atom.
bullets: Atoms were thought to be **indivisible** (could not be split)
Different elements had different atoms
No idea of any particles inside the atom

core.h: Discovery of the electron and the plum pudding model
core.p: In 1897 **J.J. Thomson** discovered the **electron**, a tiny negatively charged particle that came from inside atoms. So atoms could not be indivisible. Since atoms are neutral overall, there had to be **positive charge** too. Thomson proposed the **plum pudding model**.
bullets: Atom = a **ball of positive charge**
**Negative electrons embedded** in it, like plums (or currants) in a pudding
Positive charge and mass spread **evenly** through the whole atom
Total positive charge = total negative charge, so the atom is **neutral**
No nucleus and no empty space

callouts.p: The atom is a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded throughout it.

core.p: Around 1909, **Geiger and Marsden**, working under **Ernest Rutherford**, fired a beam of **alpha particles** (small, positively charged) at a very thin sheet of **gold foil** and recorded where they went.
bullets: Alpha source in a lead box to produce a narrow **beam**
Very **thin gold foil**: gold can be hammered extremely thin, so each alpha passes few atoms
Done in a **vacuum**, because alpha particles are absorbed by a few cm of air
A **detector** (a zinc sulfide screen that gives a tiny flash when hit) moved around the foil to count alpha particles at each angle
Prediction from the plum pudding model: the positive charge is spread out, so its force is weak and alphas should pass through with **only tiny deflections**

callouts.p: Credit is usually given for Rutherford (with Geiger and Marsden) and for the words 'alpha particles' and 'gold foil'.

core.h: Results and what each one shows
core.p: Most results matched what you might expect, but a few were astonishing: some alpha particles **bounced back**. Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back. Each observation leads to one conclusion.
bullets: **Most** alpha particles went **straight through**, so the atom is **mostly empty space**
**Some** were **deflected** through small angles, so the centre of the atom is **positively charged** (it repels the positive alpha)
**Very few** (about 1 in 8000) **bounced back** through more than 90 degrees, so the positive charge and **most of the mass** are concentrated in a **tiny volume** - the **nucleus**

head: Observation
Conclusion about the atom
rows: Nucleus is tiny, dense and contains most of the mass

callouts.p: Learn each observation with its conclusion as a pair: this is where most marks are.

core.h: Why the plum pudding model had to go
core.p: In the plum pudding model the positive charge is **spread thinly** across the whole atom. A spread-out charge produces only a weak force, nowhere near big enough to turn a fast, heavy alpha particle around. So **back-scattering could not be explained**, and the model was rejected.
bullets: Spread-out positive charge gives a weak repulsion
Alpha particles are fast and relatively heavy
So the plum pudding model predicts no large deflections
Only a **concentrated** positive charge with **concentrated mass** can repel an alpha back

callouts.p: The alphas bounce back because of **electrostatic repulsion** between positive charges, not because they 'hit something solid'.

core.p: Rutherford proposed the **nuclear model**: a tiny, dense, positively charged **nucleus** at the centre containing almost all the mass, with **electrons orbiting** around it at a large distance. Most of the atom is empty space.
bullets: Tiny central **nucleus**: positive, contains nearly all the mass
Electrons **orbit** the nucleus
Most of the atom is **empty space**
Explains all three scattering results
Later work showed the positive charge is carried by **protons**; Chadwick discovered the **neutron** in 1932

core.p: Rutherford's model did not explain how the electrons were arranged. Physics at the time predicted that orbiting electrons would continually **give out energy** and **spiral into the nucleus**, so atoms would collapse. It also could not explain why elements emit light only at **certain specific frequencies** (line spectra).
bullets: Orbiting electrons would lose energy and spiral inwards
Atoms would not be stable - but real atoms are
Could not explain line spectra of elements

core.p: **Niels Bohr** suggested that electrons can only orbit the nucleus in **fixed orbits** (shells) at **set distances** from the nucleus, each with a **fixed energy**. While in an orbit an electron does not lose energy, so the atom is **stable**.
bullets: Electrons occupy **fixed orbits** = **energy levels** (shells)
An electron in an orbit does **not radiate** energy
An electron moves to a **higher** orbit by **absorbing** electromagnetic radiation of exactly the right energy
It moves to a **lower** orbit by **emitting** electromagnetic radiation
Because energy levels are fixed, only certain frequencies are absorbed or emitted - this **explains line spectra**
Bohr's calculations agreed with experimental observations, so the model was accepted

callouts.p: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed orbits (energy levels) at specific distances from the nucleus.

core.h: Size of the atom and nucleus
core.p: The scattering experiment showed just how small the nucleus is compared with the whole atom.
bullets: Radius of an atom: about **1 x 10^-10 m**
Radius of the nucleus: about **1/100 000** of the atom's radius (around 1 x 10^-15 m)
If the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the centre
Nearly all the mass is in the nucleus

core.p: A comparison table is useful for 'compare' and 'describe the differences' questions.
bullets: Key differences: where the positive charge is, where the mass is, whether there is empty space, where the electrons are

core.p: Six-mark questions often ask you to describe how and why the model changed. Tell the story in order and give the **evidence** for each change.
bullets: Start: plum pudding - positive sphere with electrons embedded (after electron discovered)
Experiment: alpha particles fired at thin gold foil in a vacuum
Results: most straight through; some deflected; few bounced back
Conclusions: empty space; positive nucleus; tiny dense nucleus with most mass
So plum pudding replaced by nuclear model
Bohr: electrons in fixed orbits / energy levels, which matched observations

callouts.p: Use 'this showed that...' and 'so...' to link each observation to its conclusion: the link is what scores.

analogy.p: Imagine firing ping-pong balls through a fog that hides what is inside a large room. If the room were filled with thin candyfloss (plum pudding), every ball would get through with barely a wobble. Instead, almost all go straight through, a few swerve, and a very rare one shoots straight back: there must be a tiny, heavy, hidden object in the middle. The analogy breaks down because the alpha particles never touch the nucleus - they are turned back by electrostatic repulsion between positive charges, not by a collision.

terms.d: A simplified representation used to explain observations and make predictions.
Thomson's model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.
A tiny negatively charged particle, discovered by Thomson in 1897.
A positively charged particle equivalent to a helium nucleus; used as the 'probe' in the scattering experiment.
Experiment by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford firing alpha particles at thin gold foil.
Very thin sheet of gold used as the target so alphas pass very few atoms.
A change in direction of an alpha particle caused by repulsion from the nucleus.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of the atom containing most of its mass.
Rutherford's model: tiny positive nucleus with electrons around it and mostly empty space.
Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed orbits (energy levels) at specific distances.
A fixed orbit with a set energy that an electron can occupy.
The force pushing like charges apart; makes the positive nucleus repel alpha particles.
A space with no air; needed so alpha particles are not absorbed before reaching the foil.
Checking of scientific work by other scientists before it is accepted.

mistakes.w: Alpha particles bounced back because they hit the electrons.
mistakes.r: They were repelled by the small, positively charged nucleus; electrons are too light to deflect alphas significantly.

mistakes.w: Most alpha particles went straight through because the foil was thin.
mistakes.r: Most went straight through because the atom is mostly empty space.

mistakes.w: The plum pudding model has a nucleus.
mistakes.r: It has no nucleus: positive charge is spread throughout the atom.

mistakes.w: Rutherford discovered the electron.
mistakes.r: Thomson discovered the electron; Rutherford's experiment led to the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Some alpha particles were deflected because the nucleus is negative.
mistakes.r: Deflection shows the nucleus is positive (it repels positive alpha particles).

mistakes.w: Bohr's model says electrons can be anywhere around the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons are in fixed orbits (energy levels) at set distances from the nucleus.

mistakes.w: The experiment used beta particles.
mistakes.r: It used alpha particles fired at gold foil.

mistakes.w: Very few bounced back, which shows the nucleus is big.
mistakes.r: Very few bounced back, which shows the nucleus is very small (and dense).

exam.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
model: A sphere/ball of positive charge
With (negative) electrons embedded in it / spread throughout
exam.tip: Mention both the positive part and the electrons.

exam.q: Which particles were fired at the gold foil in Rutherford's scattering experiment?
model: Alpha particles
exam.tip: One word answer.

exam.q: Explain why the scattering experiment was carried out in a vacuum.
model: Alpha particles would be absorbed by (a few cm of) air
exam.tip: Link to alpha's short range in air.

exam.q: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What does this show about the atom?
model: The atom is mostly empty space
exam.tip: Not 'the foil is thin'.

exam.q: A few alpha particles were deflected through very large angles. Explain what this tells us about the nucleus.
model: The nucleus is positively charged (repels the alpha particles)
The nucleus is very small / charge is concentrated
The nucleus contains most of the mass (is dense)
exam.tip: Three ideas: charge, size, mass.

exam.q: Explain why the plum pudding model could not explain the results of the alpha scattering experiment.
model: In the plum pudding model positive charge (and mass) is spread out
So it would only cause small deflections; it cannot repel alphas back
exam.tip: Contrast spread-out charge with what was seen.

exam.q: Describe how Bohr changed Rutherford's model of the atom.
model: Electrons are in fixed orbits / shells / energy levels
At specific distances from the nucleus
exam.tip: The key word is 'fixed'.

exam.q: Give two differences between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model.
model: Plum pudding: positive charge spread out; nuclear: positive charge in a tiny nucleus
Plum pudding: no empty space / mass spread out; nuclear: mostly empty space / mass concentrated in nucleus
exam.tip: Each difference must state both models.

exam.q: Suggest why scientists accepted Bohr's model.
model: It explained experimental observations (e.g. line spectra / stable atoms)
Calculations / predictions from the model agreed with experiments
exam.tip: Models are accepted when they match evidence.

exam.q: The radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m. The nucleus is about 1/100 000 of this. Calculate the radius of the nucleus.
exam.tip: Dividing by 100 000 subtracts 5 from the power.

exam.q: Describe how and why the model of the atom changed from the plum pudding model to the Bohr model. (6 marks)
model: Plum pudding: ball of positive charge with electrons embedded
Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil (Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden)
Most went straight through, so atom mostly empty space
Some deflected / a few bounced back, so a small, dense, positive nucleus
Plum pudding replaced by nuclear model with electrons orbiting a nucleus
Bohr: electrons in fixed orbits / energy levels at specific distances, which agreed with observations
exam.tip: Indicative content: give the experiment, three results with conclusions, then Bohr.

worked.q: Model answer: In the scattering experiment, about 1 in 8000 alpha particles bounced back. Explain what this result tells us and why it surprised scientists.
steps: Plum pudding predicted only tiny deflections, because spread-out positive charge gives a weak force
A large repulsive force is needed to turn a fast alpha particle round
This needs positive charge and mass concentrated in a very small region
Because so few bounced back, the chance of a head-on approach is tiny, so this region is very small
worked.ans: There is a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the mass; it surprised scientists because the plum pudding model predicted no such large deflections.

worked.q: If a nucleus had a radius of 1 cm, roughly how big would the whole atom be?
steps: Atom radius is about 100 000 times nucleus radius
worked.ans: About 1 km in radius - showing the atom is mostly empty space.

worked.q: Applied example: A student says 'Rutherford's model was wrong, so scientists wasted their time'. Evaluate this statement.
steps: Rutherford's model correctly explained the alpha scattering evidence (empty space, nucleus)
It could not explain stable electron orbits or line spectra
Bohr built on it, keeping the nucleus and adding fixed energy levels
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: each model was the best explanation of the evidence at the time, and new models build on old ones as new evidence appears.

svg.cap: The Bohr model. Electrons can only be in fixed orbits (energy levels) at set distances from the nucleus. Absorbing electromagnetic radiation moves an electron to a higher level; falling to a lower level emits radiation.
